pages.c07-p01: Explain what computational thinking is and name its four parts
pages.c07-p02: Use decomposition to break down a problem and pattern recognition to spot similarities
pages.c07-p03: Use abstraction to remove unnecessary detail, using the London Underground map as an example
pages.c07-p04: Define an algorithm and represent one as a flowchart using the standard symbols
pages.c07-p05: Write simple pseudocode using sequence, selection and iteration
pages.c07-p06: Use variables in algorithms and trace an algorithm with a trace table
pages.c07-p07: Describe and carry out a linear search and a binary search
pages.c07-p08: Carry out a bubble sort on a list, pass by pass
pages.c07-p09: Compare algorithms that solve the same problem in terms of efficiency
pages.c07-p10: Find and fix errors in an algorithm using tracing and test data

q.q: Splitting 'organise sports day' into events, equipment, timings and helpers is which part of computational thinking?
q.why: Decomposition breaks a big problem into smaller, more manageable ones.

q.q: When writing toast instructions, you decide the colour of the toaster does not matter. This is...
q.why: Abstraction removes detail that does not matter to the problem.

q.q: Which statement best describes computational thinking?
o: It only matters when you are using a computer
It is a way of solving problems clearly and logically
It means thinking as quickly as a computer does
It is the name of a programming language
q.why: It is a problem-solving approach, useful with or without a computer.

q.q: Realising that toasting a crumpet works the same way as toasting bread is...
q.why: You spotted a similarity so you can reuse a solution.

q.q: '1. Put bread in toaster. 2. Push lever down. 3. Wait until golden.' Which part of computational thinking is this?
q.why: Algorithms are precise step-by-step instructions.

q.q: What does the memory aid 'Dogs Play All Afternoon' stand for?
q.why: D-P-A-A are the four parts of computational thinking.

q.q: Must the four parts of computational thinking always be used in a strict order?
o: Yes, algorithms must always come first
Yes, decomposition must always come last
No, you can move back and forth between them
No, only abstraction is ever needed
q.why: You might decompose, spot a pattern, then decompose further; the goal is a clear algorithm.

q.q: Why do employers value computational thinking?
o: People who use it can work without any computers
People who use it can type programs more quickly
People who use it never need to test their work
People can break problems down and explain solutions clearly
q.why: Breaking problems down and explaining solutions clearly is valued in many jobs.

q.q: In decomposition, what is a sub-problem?
o: A problem with no possible solution
A problem that has already been solved
A mistake found in an algorithm
A smaller part of a bigger problem
q.why: Decomposition produces sub-problems.

q.q: What should you do if a sub-problem is still too big?
o: Give it to a computer to solve
Turn it straight into a loop
q.why: Sub-problems can be decomposed again until each is easy.

q.q: Every lesson needs a teacher, a room, a class and a period. Noticing this is...
q.why: It is a similarity shared by every lesson.

q.q: A game studio decomposes a new game. How does this help the team?
o: It makes the problem bigger so everyone has a job
It removes the need for anyone to test the work
It means only one person needs to do any work
Different people can work on different parts at the same time
q.why: Sub-problems can be shared out, as with large games built by hundreds of people.

q.q: What comes next in 4, 8, 12, 16, ...?
q.why: The pattern is add 4, so 16 + 4 = 20.

q.q: Every trip letter is the same except for the pupil's name. How does pattern recognition help?
o: Write one letter and change the name each time
Remove the names so all letters are identical
Send one letter to the whole class to share
q.why: Spotting the pattern lets you reuse one solution.

q.q: Repeated patterns in a problem often become which feature of an algorithm?
q.why: 'Repeat these steps 28 times' is a loop.

q.q: Planning a museum trip is split into transport, permission letters, money and lunches. This is...
q.why: The big problem is broken into smaller sub-problems.

q.q: Why would making the school timetable in one go be almost impossible?
o: There is only one teacher who is allowed to make it each year
Timetables cannot be made using computers or software at all
There are hundreds of pupils, many teachers and rooms, and no clashes allowed
Every pupil in the school has exactly the same lessons each day
q.why: Decomposition turns it into smaller jobs tackled one at a time.

q.q: Which definition of abstraction is correct?
o: Breaking a problem into smaller parts
Removing detail that is not needed
q.why: Abstraction hides or removes unnecessary detail.

q.q: Harry Beck's Tube map kept which of these details?
o: The order of stations on each line
The exact bends of each tunnel
q.why: Passengers need the order of stops, not real distances.

q.q: Which electrical draughtsman had the idea for the abstract Tube map in 1931?
q.why: Harry Beck was an electrical draughtsman.

q.q: An app tells pupils when their bus leaves. Which detail is best removed?
q.why: It does not help anyone catch the bus.

q.q: What is left after abstraction?
o: A made-up version with false details
A simpler model of the real thing
A complete copy with every detail
q.why: Abstraction leaves a simpler but true model.

q.q: Which real feature was kept on Beck's Tube map to help people get their bearings?
q.why: Only a simplified Thames survived.

q.q: Why did Harry Beck remove the streets from the Tube map?
o: The streets changed far too often to draw accurately
There was not enough room on the page to print them
Passengers underground do not need them to make their journey
The streets were kept secret during the war years
q.why: They only need the line, the order of stops and where to change.

q.q: Which statement about abstraction is true?
o: Everything left on the model is still true
It means making up details to fill gaps
It always keeps every detail of the original
It is the same as decomposition
q.why: Only unnecessary detail goes; the stations, order and connections are real.

q.q: A fire exit plan shows corridors, doors and exits but not desks. This is an example of...
q.why: Detail not needed to escape is removed.

q.q: What is a good test for whether a detail can be removed in abstraction?
o: Would removing it stop the problem being solved?
Is it the longest piece of information?
Was it the first detail you wrote down?
q.why: If removing it does not stop the problem being solved, it can go.

q.q: What is an algorithm?
o: A diagram that only uses diamonds and arrows
A list of errors found while testing a program
A precise, ordered set of steps that solves a problem
A programming language such as C# or Python
q.why: A recipe or directions are algorithms; a program is an algorithm in a language.

q.q: Which recipe step is precise enough for an algorithm?
q.why: It has only one possible meaning.

q.q: Which of these is NOT a property of a good algorithm?
o: Its steps are in the correct order
q.why: An algorithm must be finite.

q.q: In a flowchart, what is the diamond shape used for?
q.why: A decision asks a Yes/No question.

q.q: Which flowchart shape should hold OUTPUT "Well done"?
q.why: Input and output both use the parallelogram.

q.q: A decision symbol asks 'Is mark >= 50?'. How many arrows leave it?
q.why: One labelled Yes and one labelled No.

q.q: Which symbol shows the Start and Stop of a flowchart?
q.why: Terminators mark the start and end.

q.q: total = total + 1 would go in which flowchart symbol?
q.why: A calculation is a process.

q.q: What is the job of the arrows (flow lines) in a flowchart?
o: Mark the start and end of the algorithm
Join the symbols and show the direction to follow
Show where data is input by the user
q.why: Flow lines show the direction of flow.

q.q: 'Butter the toast' is placed before 'toast the bread'. Which rule of a good algorithm is broken?
o: The steps must be in the correct order
The steps must use a flowchart
q.why: Order matters: the result would be very different.

q.q: What usually comes first when building a program?
o: Typing the code straight into C# or Python
Choosing the colours and fonts for the screen
Testing the finished program with test data
Planning the algorithm as a flowchart or pseudocode
q.why: Algorithms come before programs.

q.q: What is pseudocode?
o: Structured, code-like English for planning an algorithm
A diagram made of standard flowchart symbols
A table recording variable values step by step
A real programming language that runs on any computer
q.why: It is not a real language, so it will not run.

q.q: IF ... THEN ... ELSE ... ENDIF is an example of which building block?
q.why: Selection uses IF to choose a path.

q.q: In pseudocode, how should you read score ← 0?
q.why: The arrow means becomes.

q.q: What does <> mean in pseudocode?
o: Is less than or equal to
q.why: <> is not equal to.

q.q: What does FOR i ← 1 TO 4, OUTPUT i * 2, NEXT i output?
q.why: i is 1, 2, 3, 4 and each is doubled.

q.q: What does FOR i ← 1 TO 5, OUTPUT i * 3, NEXT i output?
q.why: The 3 times table for i = 1 to 5.

q.q: A game keeps asking for guesses until the user is right. Which loop suits this best?
q.why: A condition-controlled loop repeats until the condition changes.

q.q: Using the house points pseudocode (>= 100 Gold, ELSEIF >= 50 Silver, ELSE Keep going!), what is output for 50 points?
q.why: 50 is not >= 100, but it is >= 50.

q.q: Using the house points pseudocode, what is output for 120 points?
q.why: Only the first true condition runs.

q.q: In the mark pseudocode IF mark >= 50 THEN Pass ELSE Try again, what is output for 49?
q.why: 49 >= 50 is false, so ELSE runs.

q.q: Why are the lines inside an IF or a loop indented?
o: To show clearly which lines belong to it
To make the algorithm run faster
To mark the lines that contain errors
q.why: Indentation shows structure.

q.q: What does the sequence building block mean?
o: Steps are repeated a fixed number of times, then stop
Steps are carried out one after another, from top to bottom
Unnecessary steps are removed to keep it simple
A choice is made between paths using a condition
q.why: Sequence is running steps in order.

q.q: What is a variable?
o: A named store for a value that can change
A symbol used in a flowchart
A value that can never change once set
A table that records every step
q.why: Its value can vary while the algorithm runs.

q.q: score is 7. After score ← score + 3, what is score?
q.why: 7 + 3 = 10, which replaces the old value.

q.q: score ← 0, then score ← score + 5, then score ← score + 5. What is output by OUTPUT score?
Why would you draw a trace table?
o: Sorting a list into ascending order
Storing the passwords of every user
Recording variable values step by step during a dry run
Drawing the symbols of a flowchart neatly
q.why: It tracks every value as you work through by hand.

q.q: How many times does the loop body run in WHILE count <= 4, if count starts at 1 and goes up by 1 each pass?
q.why: count = 1, 2, 3, 4 pass; 5 fails.

q.q: total ← 0, count ← 1, WHILE count <= 4: total ← total + count, count ← count + 1. What is output for total?
Which variable name follows the advice on this page for storing a test mark?
q.why: Meaningful, no spaces, does not start with a number.

q.q: What is working through an algorithm by hand, line by line, called?
q.why: A dry run is recorded in a trace table.

q.q: A variable holds 12. The algorithm runs total ← 5. What does the variable hold now?
q.why: A variable holds one value at a time; the new value replaces the old one.

q.q: When working out score ← score + 5, what should you do first?
o: Work out the right-hand side using the old value
q.why: It is not an equation: calculate, then store.

q.q: Before a binary search can be used, the list must be...
o: It must have fewer than 100 items
q.why: Halving only works if the items are in order.

q.q: A linear search for 8 in 4, 9, 8, 2 checks how many items?
q.why: It checks 4, then 9, then finds 8 at the third check.

q.q: In a binary search, low = 1 and high = 10. Which position is checked first?
You have an unsorted list of names. Which search can you use?
q.why: Binary search needs a sorted list; linear search does not.

q.q: How does a linear search work?
o: It checks the middle item and halves the list
It sorts the list first, then checks the end
It checks each item in turn from the start
It checks the last item and works backwards in halves
q.why: It starts at the first item until it finds the target or reaches the end.

q.q: In a binary search, the middle item is smaller than the target. What happens next?
o: The lower half is thrown away
The upper half is thrown away
The search starts again at position 1
q.why: The target must be in the upper half.

q.q: Which everyday task works most like a binary search?
o: Counting the pupils in a register
Finding a word in a dictionary
Checking every coat on a coat rack
q.why: Open in the middle, then decide which half to look in.

q.q: Why does a binary search fail on an unsorted list?
o: It can only search lists of numbers
It could throw away the half that contains the target
It always checks every item twice
It cannot find the middle of the list
q.why: Halving assumes items are in order.

q.q: A binary search has low = 6 and high = 9. Which position is checked next?
q.why: (6 + 9) DIV 2 = 15 DIV 2 = 7, rounding down.

q.q: A linear search for 12 in 5, 7, 3, 9 finishes. What is output?
q.why: Every item is checked and none is 12.

q.q: In a bubble sort, what happens to the largest item in pass 1?
o: It moves to the end of the list
q.why: It is swapped along every time until it reaches the end.

q.q: How does a bubble sort know the list is sorted?
o: When a whole pass makes no swaps
After as many passes as there are items
When the first item is the smallest
q.why: No swaps in a pass means everything is in order.

q.q: What is 3, 1, 2 after one pass of a bubble sort into ascending order?
q.why: 3 and 1 swap (1, 3, 2), then 3 and 2 swap (1, 2, 3).

q.q: Why is a temporary variable needed to swap two values?
o: So the algorithm counts the number of passes
So the largest value is deleted from the list
So one value is not lost when it is overwritten
So the list is sorted into descending order
q.why: Like the empty cup when swapping two drinks.

q.q: What does ascending order mean?
o: In the order items were entered
q.why: Ascending is 1, 2, 3 or A to Z.

q.q: How many comparisons does one pass of a bubble sort make on a list of 5 items?
q.why: 5 items have 4 neighbouring pairs.

q.q: What is 5, 2, 8, 1, 4 after pass 1 of a bubble sort into ascending order?
What is 4, 3, 2, 1 after one pass of a bubble sort into ascending order?
q.why: 4 is swapped along to the end: 3, 4, 2, 1 → 3, 2, 4, 1 → 3, 2, 1, 4.

q.q: After pass 3, the list 5, 2, 8, 1, 4 looks sorted. Why is pass 4 still needed?
o: Pass 4 checks that the list is also in descending order
Every bubble sort of five items must make exactly four passes
The algorithm only knows it is finished when a pass makes no swaps
Pass 4 is the pass that moves the smallest item to the start
q.why: Pass 3 made a swap, so another pass is needed to confirm.

q.q: In the pseudocode, which condition decides whether two neighbours swap?
q.why: Swap if the left item is bigger, for ascending order.

q.q: When computer scientists compare the efficiency of algorithms, what are they comparing?
o: Which language it is written in
How much time and memory it uses
q.why: Efficient algorithms use fewer steps and less memory.

q.q: A sorted list has 1,000 items. What is the most checks a binary search needs?
q.why: Halving 1,000 repeatedly takes at most 10 checks.

q.q: In which situation is a linear search a sensible choice?
o: The list contains a million items
The target is in the middle
The list is short or unsorted
The list is huge and sorted
q.why: No sorting needed, and on a short list the difference is tiny.

q.q: What is the worst case for a linear search on a list of 50 items?
q.why: The target is last, or missing, so every item is checked.

q.q: Why do computer scientists count steps rather than use a stopwatch?
o: A faster computer would give a different time
Stopwatches are not allowed in computing
Algorithms cannot be timed at all
Counting steps is always quicker to do
q.why: Counting steps compares the algorithms, not the computers.

q.q: The size of a sorted list doubles. What happens to the worst case for a binary search?
o: It needs half as many checks
It needs twice as many checks
q.why: Each check halves what is left.

q.q: A sorted list has 1,000,000 items. What is the worst case for a binary search?
q.why: The table gives 20 checks for a million items.

q.q: What is the best case for a binary search?
o: 1 check, when the target is first
1 check, when the target is in the middle
q.why: For a linear search the best case is when the target is first.

q.q: Algorithm A adds 1 to 100 in a loop; algorithm B uses n * (n + 1) / 2. Which is more efficient?
o: A, because loops are always the fastest method
B, because it takes a few steps however big n is
A, because it gives a more accurate answer
B, because it uses a loop of 100 steps
q.why: Both are correct, but the formula takes far fewer steps.

q.q: Why is bubble sort slow on big lists?
o: It uses a binary search for every item
It needs the list to be sorted first
It keeps passing through the whole list
q.why: Faster methods such as merge sort are used for big jobs.

q.q: An algorithm has no errors in its keywords and runs, but outputs the wrong total. What type of error is this?
q.why: It follows the rules but the logic is wrong.

q.q: count ← 1, then WHILE count <= 3 with only OUTPUT count inside. What happens?
q.why: count never changes, so it is an infinite loop.

q.q: The rule is 'pass if 50 or more'. Which pair is boundary test data?
q.why: They sit either side of the edge of the rule.

q.q: WHILE count < 10 should output 1 to 10 but stops at 9. What kind of bug is this?
q.why: It runs one time too few; <= fixes it.

q.q: OUPTUT score is an example of which kind of error?
q.why: A misspelt keyword breaks the rules of the language.

q.q: Why is a logic error harder to find than a syntax error?
o: The algorithm still runs, so nothing points to the mistake
Logic errors stop the algorithm from running at all
The editor points to the line of every logic error
Logic errors only happen on very old computers
q.why: You only notice when the answer is wrong.

q.q: The broken average algorithm uses total ← mark inside the loop. With marks 6, 8, 10, 7, 9 it outputs 1.8. What is the fix?
q.why: total ← mark keeps only the last mark (9), and 9 / 5 = 1.8.

q.q: IF mark > 50 is used for 'pass if 50 or more'. What happens to a mark of exactly 50?
o: It fails, though it should pass
q.why: A wrong comparison: it should be >= 50.

q.q: Which is erroneous test data for a mark out of 100?
q.why: Erroneous values, like 150, should be rejected.

q.q: Why should you work out the expected output before testing?
o: So you can skip the trace table
Because the algorithm needs it as input
So the test runs more quickly
Otherwise you cannot tell if the algorithm got it wrong
q.why: You need the right answer to compare with.
